description: A group of three bright-field transmission electron micrographs (no printed (a)/(b)/(c) letters) showing dislocation structures in Fe–20% Al deformed to 2–3%. All three show dark, thin, smoothly curved single dislocation lines on a mottled bright-grey matrix; no cell walls or dense tangles dominate. Top panel: a diagonal arrow at the lower right marks the imaging vector (g ∥ 011) and a printed scale bar reads 0.25 µm; several short segmented, dipole-like traces appear among the bowed lines. Middle panel: the same curled single dislocations, with a horizontal arrow pointing left at the lower right, i.e. the opposite-sign imaging vector; no scale bar is legible here. Bottom panel: a denser field of curved dislocations carrying about ten printed "d" annotations marking individual dislocation dipoles, a horizontal right-pointing arrow, and a printed scale bar of 0.2 µm. The caption states the zone axis (stress axis) is [0 1 1], that opposite-sign imaging vectors were used for the two photographs, and that the relative image displacement d demonstrates the dipole character of many segments and of occasional small loops. The figure demonstrates that in disordered/short-range-ordered Fe–20% Al, plasticity is carried by individually gliding, curved (1/2)⟨111⟩ dislocations that trail edge dipoles and loops.

observations.observation: The figure group consists of three separate TEM micrographs presented in reading order (top, middle, bottom); no (a)/(b)/(c) letters are printed on any of them.
The top micrograph carries a printed scale bar reading '0.25µm' and a diagonal arrow at the lower right that marks the imaging-vector direction.
The middle micrograph has a solid horizontal arrow at the lower right pointing to the left (opposite imaging-vector sense to the bottom panel); no scale bar is visible in this panel.
The bottom micrograph carries a printed scale bar reading '0.2µm' and a solid horizontal arrow pointing to the right.
The bottom micrograph is annotated with roughly ten small printed 'd' labels distributed over the field, each beside a short dislocation segment or small loop trace.

In all three micrographs the dislocations appear as long, smoothly curved, individually resolved lines rather than as dense tangles or well-developed cell walls; no precipitates or second-phase particles are evident.
The background in all three panels is mottled with darker and brighter patches (foil-thickness/diffraction contrast), separating regions of higher and lower dislocation density.
The caption states the zone axis (stress axis) is [0 1 1] and the imaging vector (arrowed) is parallel to 011.

The caption states that opposite-sign imaging vectors were used for the two photographs and that the relative displacement of the images (indicated as d) demonstrates the dipole arrangement of many dislocation segments and loops.
The caption identifies the material as Fe–20% Al and the imaged objects as curled single dislocations.

The citing text states the structures were observed after straining to 2–3% and that disordered or short-range-ordered Fe–Al is deformed by movement of single dislocations of Burgers vector (1/2)⟨1 1 1⟩, as in Figs. 5–7 for 15 and 20% Al.
The citing text states that many of the bowed dislocations in Fig. 6, and many segments in clustered regions of Fig. 5, were seen to be dipoles, with occasional small loops.

The citing text contrasts Fig. 6 with the Fe–25% Al (DO3-ordered) material, where dislocation pairs remain straighter and closer to screw orientation, the loops and dipoles there being trailed from gliding screw dislocations.
